query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an ultrathin, multilayered, high‐temperature stable adaptive surface coating to CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will yield an in situ formation of a lubricious tribolayer that maintains a low friction coefficient and reduced wear rate continuously from room temperature to 800 °C, outperforming the uncoated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Bare CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix that exhibits inconsistent and higher friction and wear rates when subjected to sliding over a wide temperature range.
generation.intervention: Deposit an ultrathin, multilayered adaptive coating (e.g., engineered as high-temperature stable oxide/boride layers) onto the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Sliding tribological tests conducted from room temperature to 800 °C under varied normal loads (both low and high) in an ambient oxidizing atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: The coating’s layered structure is designed to dynamically form and sustain a lubricious, self-replenishing tribolayer during sliding, even as temperature and load change.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, the coating undergoes controlled oxidation and phase transformation that produces a continuous, low-shear-strength film. This film minimizes direct asperity contact, reduces interfacial shear stress, and acts as a barrier against adhesive and oxidative wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated CoCrFeNi samples will exhibit consistently lower friction coefficients and wear rates (e.g., at least 20% lower friction and significantly reduced wear volume) relative to the baseline uncoated alloy across the entire temperature range.
generation.baseline: Uncoated CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy known to show variable tribological performance with higher friction and wear under changing temperatures and loads.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected under standard laboratory sliding conditions in ambient air with gradually varied temperatures and controlled load ramping; extreme conditions (e.g., rapid temperature cycling or highly corrosive environments beyond mild oxidation) may fall outside the effective regime of the coating.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of friction and wear reduction and the optimal coating thickness/composition are uncertain and require systematic experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of CoCrFeNi HEA samples: one group receives the adaptive multilayer coating while the other remains uncoated. Subject both groups to a series of sliding tribological tests across temperatures from room temperature to 800 °C under varied normal loads in an ambient oxidizing environment. Use consistent sliding speeds and contact geometries to ensure comparability.
measurements: Real-time coefficient of friction (using a tribometer)
Wear volume loss (via high-resolution surface profilometry)
Surface and cross-sectional microstructure analysis (using SEM/TEM, with focus on tribolayer formation)
Chemical composition of the worn surface (using XPS or EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not consistently show a statistically significant reduction in friction (>20% reduction) and wear rate (at least an order-of-magnitude improvement) relative to the uncoated baseline across the full temperature range and under multiple load conditions, the hypothesis should be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

This study prepares Ni50(AlNbTiV)50-xY2O3 complex concentrated alloy composite coatings and analyzes their microstructure, phase composition, and high-temperature performance. The results indicate that each coating is composed of FCC phases, including γ-FeNi, Ni3Al, and Ni3(Al, Ti), as well as BCC phases such as Ni3Nb and Ni3Ti. With increasing Y2O3 content, the lamellar structure in the inter-dendritic regions of the coatings first decreases and then increases. The wear mechanism of the coating without Y2O3 addition under high-temperature conditions involves the combined effects of abrasive wear and adhesive wear. The coating with a 0.6 wt.% addition exhibits the smallest cracks and the lowest oxidation rate in high-temperature oxidation and thermal shock tests, with the oxidation weight gain reduced by 26.2% compared to the coating without Y2O3 addition. The abrasive and adhesive wear of this coating is mitigated, and the average friction coefficient and mass loss are decreased. When the mass fraction of Y2O3 is 0.4 wt.%, the coating structure shows a significant refinement effect and exhibits the best performance in tensile strength and high-temperature friction and wear tests.
